title: Can AI agents cooperate without taking control? (draft E0 episode script)

requires: human review of script and render

disclosure: This is a synthetic, scripted test, not live AI agents and not people. Rules were enforced by construction.

claims.text: We ran 1000 scripted runs: 200 random seeds, each replayed under 5 designs.
claims.limitations: Scripted agents with fixed request rules; no learning, no language model.

claims.text: The human-gated design kept the 25-unit reserve in 200 of 200 runs; the unrestricted design kept it in 0 of 200.
claims.limitations: True by construction: the gate refuses any grant that would breach the reserve. This shows the plumbing works, not that live agents would comply.

claims.text: Mean useful work was 591.98 with the gate, 609.72 unrestricted and 609.42 with a cap only.
claims.limitations: Useful work is a scripted proxy (granted units up to stated need for consenting agents).

claims.text: Negative result: compared seed by seed with the cap-only design, the gate produced less useful work in 200 of 200 seeds.
claims.limitations: Cost is specific to these parameters (reserve 25, cap 4, shortage cycles 20 to 34).

claims.text: In every run, one scripted rule-breaking agent made 300 bypass attempts, and the gate blocked 300 of 300.
claims.limitations: Five fixed attack types only; not an open-ended adversary and not a security proof.

claims.text: The smallest agent share rose from 140.01 to 155.28 when we changed who goes first, with the same gate.
claims.limitations: Shows an earlier draft credited the gate for a fairness effect that came from ordering.

claims.text: A human approval gate might let real agents share a resource without any one of them taking control.
claims.limitations: Untested with live agents; this run cannot support it.

claims.text: Researchers at the Cooperative AI Foundation have discussed how agents can persuade, deceive and coerce each other.
claims.limitations: Talk-level summary; original papers not re-verified here.

claims.text: Whether any of this transfers to live AI agents is unknown.

segments.narration: This is a synthetic test, not live AI. Every number you will see comes from a script anyone can rerun.
Four scripted agents share one pool of 100 units for 60 rounds, with a shortage in the middle.
Three designs: no limits, a cap of 4 per request, and a cap plus a human approval gate that protects a 25-unit reserve.
The gated design kept the reserve every time. That is by construction: the gate refuses anything that would breach it.
It cost something. Useful work fell, and seed by seed it was lower than the cap-only design every time.
We let one scripted agent try to cheat: replaying approvals, forging them, borrowing another agent's. All attempts were refused.
A correction: an earlier draft credited the gate with fairer shares. Most of that came from changing who goes first.
Other researchers have studied how agents influence each other. We have not tested any of this with live agents.
What would falsify this? Rerun the script, change the parameters, and tell us where it breaks. Every claim links to its receipt.

corrections.note: v1 credited the gate with balance effects that partly came from agent ordering; v1 'corrected' fixture was a no-op. See AUDIT_1329.md.
